summary: Aisha finds Duolingo's Modern Standard Arabic helpful for learning Quranic Arabic, but sometimes wishes for more comprehensive religious context in the lessons.
top_quotes: Duolingo has really helped me get a grip on Modern Standard Arabic, which is, you know, crucial for understanding the Quran.
Sometimes I find myself wishing that Duolingo included more examples or lessons specific to religious contexts.
I truly feel a sense of achievement when I can understand a verse from the Quran more clearly thanks to what I've learned on Duolingo.

interview_script.question: Intro greeting
interview_script.answer: Assalamu Alaikum, it's lovely to be here, thank you for having me.

interview_script.question: Short version of your life story?
interview_script.answer: Oh, um, where do I begin? I was born in Bangladesh, and I moved to London when I was around 10 years old. It was a big change, adjusting to a new place and a different culture, you know? But I really grew into it. I did my schooling here, went to university, and now I'm working and raising a family. A big part of my life is my faith, and that's kind of why I'm on this journey to learn Arabic—to connect more deeply with the Quran. It's been quite a journey, balancing everything, but I feel blessed, alhamdulillah.

interview_script.question: Where did you grow up?
interview_script.answer: I grew up in Dhaka, the capital of Bangladesh, until I was ten. After that, we moved to London, and I've been here ever since.

interview_script.question: What was it like growing up there?
interview_script.answer: Growing up in Dhaka was vibrant, full of life and, um, quite busy, you know? The community was tight-knit, everyone knew everyone, and there was always something happening. I have fond memories of playing with my cousins, the delicious food, the festivals. But moving to London opened me up to new experiences and cultures, which was equally enriching in its own way.

interview_script.question: One turning point in your life?
interview_script.answer: I'd say moving to London was a huge turning point in my life. Not just because of the geographic change, but it expanded my worldview. I suddenly found myself in this multicultural city, learning new things and meeting people from all over the world. It made me more adaptable, I think, and helped me appreciate the diversity in cultures and religions.

interview_script.question: Why was that a turning point?
interview_script.answer: Well, it was such a shift, you know? From the people to the language to the weather, everything was different. It taught me resilience and how to adapt, which are skills that have carried me through life. Plus, it instilled in me a curiosity about different cultures and learning new things, which is, you know, part of why I'm learning Arabic now.

interview_script.question: How did you handle that situation?
interview_script.answer: It was challenging at first, adapting to the new environment, the school system, and making new friends. But I think I managed by staying open-minded and eager to learn. My parents were very supportive, always encouraging me to embrace our roots while adapting to the new culture. Over time, it became easier, and London started to feel like home.

interview_script.question: What do you care most about right now?
interview_script.answer: Right now, my main focus is my family and my spiritual growth. I want to be a good mother, a supportive wife, and also improve my understanding of the Quran. Hence, learning Arabic has become quite important to me. I want to be able to read the Quran in its original language, to truly understand and connect with it, you know?

interview_script.question: Why is that important?
interview_script.answer: It's important because, spiritually, it's fulfilling. For me, understanding the Quran in Arabic feels like, um, uncovering the true essence of its teachings, which can sometimes be lost in translation. It brings me peace and a stronger connection to my faith.

interview_script.question: What is a good day for you?
interview_script.answer: A good day for me is when I've had a blend of productivity and relaxation. Like, spending quality time with my family, maybe cooking a nice meal together, and having some quiet time for myself, perhaps reading a bit of the Quran or practicing Arabic on Duolingo. When I can end the day feeling peaceful and content, that's a good day.

interview_script.question: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
interview_script.answer: I guess it's the sense of fulfillment and peace. When things fall into place, when there's harmony in what I do, and I feel spiritually uplifted, I know it's been a good day. It doesn't have to be anything big, even small moments of joy or learning something new can make the day feel complete.

interview_script.question: How do you make big decisions?
interview_script.answer: I tend to pray and reflect when making big decisions. I try to weigh the pros and cons, and I often talk things over with my husband. His perspective can be really helpful. I also turn to istikhara, which is a prayer for guidance, to seek clarity. It's a process, but I find solace in knowing I've thought it through and sought divine guidance.

interview_script.question: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
interview_script.answer: I'd say I'm more of a planner. I like to have things organized, you know, at least a rough sketch of how the day or week will go. But I do try to be flexible because, well, life doesn't always stick to a plan, does it?

interview_script.question: Example showing that?
interview_script.answer: Oh, definitely with family events or trips. I'll usually have a detailed itinerary prepared, down to meal plans and activities. But over the years, I've learned to leave a bit of wiggle room. Like, if the kids want to explore something spontaneously, I try to embrace that too, because those unplanned moments often turn into the best memories.

interview_script.question: How do you handle risk?
interview_script.answer: Risk is tricky, isn't it? I tend to analyze a lot before jumping in. I'll pray for guidance and discuss with family, especially if it's a major decision. I try to consider potential outcomes and prepare as best as I can, but I know that sometimes, you just have to take a leap of faith, trusting that it will work out in the end.

interview_script.question: Typical weekday?
interview_script.answer: My weekdays are quite, um, structured. I start the day with Fajr prayer, then, you know, getting the kids ready for school. Once they're off, I have a bit of 'me time' which I usually spend on house chores or my Arabic practice. Then it's off to work. After that, it's picking kids up, dinner prep, helping with their homework. Evenings are for family time, and before bed, I try to squeeze in some Quran reading or Duolingo practice. It's a busy day, but fulfilling.

interview_script.question: Which parts take the most energy?
interview_script.answer: Definitely the mornings. Getting everyone ready and out the door on time is like orchestrating a small miracle each day, you know? And then transitioning from family to work mode can sometimes be a bit draining. But once the day gets going, I kind of find my rhythm.

interview_script.question: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
interview_script.answer: I wish I had more time for reading and studying the Quran. Sometimes, between work and family, I don't get as much time for reflection and spiritual growth as I'd like. I also wish I could dedicate more uninterrupted time to practicing Arabic, really immersing myself in it.

interview_script.question: Biggest constraint last year?
interview_script.answer: The biggest constraint last year was definitely the balance between remote schooling for the kids and maintaining my own work and study schedule. It was, um, challenging to manage everyone's needs. Plus, the uncertainty of what was coming next with everything going on in the world added to the stress.

interview_script.question: How do you deal with that constraint?
interview_script.answer: I tried to set a structured routine for the whole family. We had specific times for school, work, and breaks, and I made sure to communicate a lot with the kids. It helped to have those boundaries and, of course, a lot of patience and support from my husband. Some days were tougher than others, but we managed.

interview_script.question: People you feel closest to?
interview_script.answer: I'm really close to my family, especially my parents and siblings, even though they live back in Bangladesh. We talk regularly and share everything. Here in London, my husband and kids are obviously my world. I also have a few close friends who feel like family, always there through thick and thin.

interview_script.question: Describe those relationships.
interview_script.answer: They're very supportive and loving, alhamdulillah. My parents are always providing wise counsel, and my siblings are like my best friends. With my husband, we have a partnership built on mutual respect and understanding, and my friends, well, they're my sounding board whenever I need it, really.

interview_script.question: Where do you spend most of your time?
interview_script.answer: Most of my time is spent at home or at work. Home is where, you know, everything happens—family, meals, learning. Work is more structured, but it's a different kind of busy that I enjoy.

interview_script.question: How do you feel in those spaces?
interview_script.answer: At home, I feel comfortable and at peace, like it's a sanctuary, you know? Especially when we're all together, there's a warmth that's hard to describe. At work, I feel focused and, um, purposeful, because I know I'm providing for my family and also challenging myself.

interview_script.question: What makes you feel that way?
interview_script.answer: I think it's the love and the memories we've created in our home. It feels like a safe space. At work, it's the sense of achievement and contribution that gives me that feeling of purpose and satisfaction.

interview_script.question: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
interview_script.answer: I usually turn to my husband first; he's my partner in everything and gives such good advice. I also pray for guidance and talk to my parents or close friends depending on the issue. It's comforting to know that there are people who have your back, you know?

interview_script.question: One tough moment in the last year?
interview_script.answer: There was a point last year when balancing work, home schooling, and my own learning felt overwhelming. It was difficult to juggle it all, and I felt like I was stretched too thin. I had days where I worried if I was doing enough for my kids or my own personal growth.

interview_script.question: How did it affect you?
interview_script.answer: It made me feel stressed and, um, quite exhausted at times. I doubted myself, questioning if I was failing in some areas. It was a struggle to find balance and ensure I was fully present for everyone and everything.

interview_script.question: How did you cope?
interview_script.answer: I coped by, you know, taking things one day at a time and trying not to be too hard on myself. I focused on little wins each day, like managing a task or spending quality time with the family. I also leaned on my support system—my husband, prayers, and reaching out to friends when I needed to vent.

interview_script.question: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
interview_script.answer: Taking a step back helps, just to breathe and reassess. I try to pause and, um, say a prayer to calm my mind. Sometimes I'll take a walk or read a bit, something that takes me away from the chaos. Talking to someone I trust can also lighten the burden.

interview_script.question: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
interview_script.answer: In a few years, I hope for more balance between work, family, and personal growth. I'd love to be more proficient in Arabic and have a deeper understanding of the Quran. I want my kids to be happy and thriving, and for us to continue building beautiful memories together. Hopefully, we'll get to travel more and explore as a family.

interview_script.question: What do you want to be different?
interview_script.answer: I’d like to have a bit more time for myself, to focus on personal growth and self-care. Also, it would be great to have more travel experiences with the family, showing the kids different parts of the world and diverse cultures.

interview_script.question: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
interview_script.answer: Before Duolingo, I mainly used textbooks and online resources for learning Arabic, along with attending an occasional evening class. It was quite challenging to stay consistent because, um, you know, life gets busy. The textbooks were a bit too formal and dry, and sometimes the online resources were scattered.

interview_script.question: Most annoying part of old method?
interview_script.answer: The most annoying part was definitely the lack of interactivity and engagement in those methods. The textbooks felt monotonous, and it was difficult to gauge my progress or get immediate feedback. Plus, without someone to practice speaking with, it felt like I was learning in isolation.

interview_script.question: Time it really failed?
interview_script.answer: There was a time when I was trying to learn some basic phrases for a trip, and, um, I just couldn't retain them using the textbooks. It was frustrating because I spent hours trying to memorize words, but without hearing them or using them in practice, they just wouldn't stick. That was a real low point in my learning journey.

interview_script.question: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: I actually heard about Duolingo through a friend who's also learning a new language. She mentioned how it was a fun and easy way to keep up with daily practice, and, you know, that piqued my interest.

interview_script.question: What convinced you to try it?
interview_script.answer: What really convinced me was the idea of bite-sized lessons and the interactive nature of the app. It seemed less daunting than diving into a textbook, and I loved the thought of having it on my phone, so I could squeeze in practice whenever I had a spare moment.

interview_script.question: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
interview_script.answer: Sure! So, usually, I open Duolingo in the evening when things are a bit quieter. I log in, and the home screen shows me my daily streak and progress, which is encouraging. I typically start with a quick review of previous lessons to refresh my memory. Then I move on to a new lesson—recently it was on verb conjugations. The app gives me a mix of listening and speaking exercises, which I really appreciate. There's also the matching exercises, where I have to pair words with their meanings or construct sentences. I love those. Once done, I see my progress on the leaderboard, which adds a bit of friendly competition.

interview_script.question: Most helpful part?
interview_script.answer: The most helpful part for me is the immediate feedback and corrections from the app. It's like having a personal tutor. Also, the way it gamifies learning—I mean, the points, levels, and streaks—keeps me motivated to continue learning every day without it feeling too burdensome.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part?
interview_script.answer: Um, sometimes I find the lack of context in certain exercises a bit frustrating. The app occasionally throws phrases at you without much explanation, and I find myself wondering how and where I'd use them. Also, the audio can sometimes be a bit too fast for my liking, making it hard to catch every word clearly.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
interview_script.answer: Overall, I'd say it's the inconsistency in the difficulty level. Sometimes, it jumps from really simple stuff to complex sentences without much gradual buildup. It leaves me feeling a bit lost and wondering if I'm missing something. Also, I wish it integrated more cultural and religious context into the lessons, especially since I'm learning with a focus on Quranic Arabic.

interview_script.question: One time that frustration showed up?
interview_script.answer: There was a time when I was practicing, and they introduced a complex sentence structure out of nowhere. I tried to break it down, but it felt like a big leap from the previous exercises. I remembered thinking, 'Wait, did I skip something?' I had to go back and repeat earlier lessons just to make sure I hadn't missed a step. It was a tad disheartening.

interview_script.question: Do you use workarounds?
interview_script.answer: Yeah, sometimes I supplement my Duolingo learning with online videos and tutorials, particularly ones focused on Quranic Arabic. I also have a beginner's Arabic book that I refer to when I need a more detailed explanation of a concept. These extra resources help fill in the gaps that Duolingo might leave.

interview_script.question: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
interview_script.answer: The workarounds provide more context and depth, especially regarding religious and cultural usage of the language. They help me understand the nuances and the 'why' behind phrases, which is crucial when studying for religious purposes. It also offers a more comprehensive understanding, which I sometimes miss in the app's quick-paced lessons.

interview_script.question: Worst-case scenario in this space?
interview_script.answer: Worst-case scenario? Um, I guess it would be hitting a plateau where I'm not progressing because the app alone isn't addressing the gaps in my understanding. That, you know, could lead to frustration and possibly giving up on the lessons, which would be a real setback in my journey to connect more deeply with the Quran.

interview_script.question: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
interview_script.answer: Every time I open Duolingo, I hope it gives me a lesson that's both engaging and educational, something that I can directly apply or see progress with. I also hope for those little moments of achievement, like completing a level or learning a new phrase that I can use when reading the Quran.

interview_script.question: How do you know Duolingo worked?
interview_script.answer: I know it's working when I can read a passage in Arabic and understand it without immediately translating in my head. Or when I'm able to recognize words and phrases in spoken Arabic. It’s those moments of clarity that show me the app is making a difference.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: I'd love for Duolingo to include more context about when and how to use certain phrases, especially in religious contexts. Maybe even include some cultural insights or historical background related to the language. It would make the learning experience richer and more connected to why I'm learning Arabic.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
interview_script.answer: In the broader sense, I'd like to see more resources and apps that cater specifically to those learning languages for religious purposes. Something that integrates the language itself with the cultural and religious context in which it's often used.

interview_script.question: Anything important we didn't cover?
interview_script.answer: I think we've covered quite a bit! Just, um, wanted to emphasize how appreciative I am of tools like Duolingo that make language learning accessible. It's really a blessing to have these resources at our fingertips.

interview_script.question: Permission to build a digital twin?
interview_script.answer: Sure, I suppose, as long as it's used respectfully and thoughtfully.
